Repipe Cost Guide: What a Whole House Repipe Really Costs

By SRQ Leak Pros Editorial · Published November 5, 2026 · Updated November 7, 2026 · 5 min read

Short answer: Angi puts a whole house repipe at about $1,500 to $15,000, with a typical cost near $7,500. Your repipe cost depends on home size, the number of fixtures, the pipe you choose and how much wall and ceiling has to be opened and patched. Ask for written quotes that list drywall repair, permits and inspection.

A repipe is one of the larger plumbing bills a homeowner faces, so the repipe cost question comes early. It usually follows repeat leaks, failing polybutylene or old galvanized pipe. If you're weighing it, SRQ Leak Pros can connect you with a local provider for repiping in Sarasota who can price your home.

This is general information to help you compare bids, not a quote. Prices vary by home and by provider.

How much does a whole house repipe cost?

Angi's cost guide, updated July 2026, puts most whole house repipes between about $1,500 and $15,000. It lists a typical project at about $7,500. A small home with one bathroom and easy attic access sits at the low end. A large two-story home with many fixtures and finished ceilings sits at the high end.

These are national figures. Use them to sanity-check a Sarasota quote, not to set one.

What drives repipe cost?

FactorWhy it matters
Square footage and layoutMore pipe and more runs
Number of bathrooms and fixturesEach fixture needs a supply line and a new valve
Pipe materialPEX usually costs less to buy and install than copper
AccessOpen attics are faster; slabs and finished ceilings take longer
Wall and ceiling repairDrywall patching and paint may or may not be in the quote
StoriesTwo-story homes need vertical runs through walls
Permits and inspectionUsually required for a full repipe
ExtrasNew shut-offs, a pressure reducing valve or water heater connections

PEX vs. copper vs. CPVC: does pipe choice change the price?

Yes, often by a lot. PEX is cross-linked polyethylene. Wikipedia notes it's widely used for water supply lines. It bends around corners, so it needs fewer fittings and fewer wall openings. Copper is rigid metal pipe that costs more for material and labor. CPVC is a rigid plastic used for hot and cold lines.

PipeInstall speedRelative costNotes
PEXFast; flexible runsLowerFewer joints; keep away from UV light
CopperSlower; soldered jointsHigherCan develop pinhole leaks over time
CPVCModerate; glued jointsMiddleRigid; can grow brittle with age

Ask each bidder which pipe they plan to use and why.

What hidden repipe costs should you plan for?

These items often decide whether a low bid stays low:

  • Drywall patching. Some quotes stop at rough patches. Others include texture and paint.
  • Permits. A full repipe usually needs a permit and inspection.
  • Fixture valves. New angle stops under sinks and toilets are often included, but ask.
  • Water heater connections. New lines to the heater may be extra.
  • Hose bibs. Outdoor faucets may or may not be replaced.
  • Slab work. If supply lines run under the slab, the plan may reroute them overhead.
  • Water shut-offs. Ask whether water will be back on each night of the job.

Is a repipe worth the cost?

Often, yes, when leaks keep coming back. Each patch costs money and risks water damage. A repipe also clears out known problem pipe such as polybutylene. Wikipedia notes polybutylene can break down when exposed to chlorine in water and is no longer accepted by U.S. building codes. Some insurers may ask about it too.

A repipe may not be worth it if the leaks trace to one bad section, high pressure or a single failed fitting. A good provider will tell you when a targeted repair makes more sense.

Repipe vs. spot repairs

SituationBetter fit
One leak in otherwise sound pipeSpot repair
Several leaks in a yearRepipe quote
Polybutylene throughoutRepipe
Slab leak in older copperReroute or repipe
Rusty water and low flow from galvanizedRepipe

Florida rules for a repipe

Florida places water supply work within a plumbing contractor's scope under § 489.105(3)(m) of the Florida Statutes. Use a licensed plumbing contractor and check the license on the DBPR site. Expect a permit and an inspection. Ask who pulls the permit and whether the inspection fee is in the price.

What affects repipe cost in Sarasota?

Many Sarasota homes are single-story on a concrete slab, with supply lines under the floor or in the attic. Attic runs are often easier to replace. Lines under the slab are usually rerouted overhead instead of dug out. Summer attic heat can slow the work and affect scheduling. Condos and older coastal homes may need building approval and tighter work hours.

How to get a fair repipe quote

  1. Get two or three written quotes. Ask for the same pipe type in each.
  2. Compare scope line by line. Fixtures, valves, heater lines and hose bibs.
  3. Ask about walls. Who patches, and to what finish?
  4. Confirm the schedule. How many days, and is water on each night?
  5. Check the warranty. Ask what it covers and for how long.
  6. Verify the license. Look up the contractor on the DBPR site.

Local note: older homes in Venice and Bradenton are common repipe candidates when original pipe ages out. Newer homes in Lakewood Ranch seldom need a full repipe but may need targeted fixes.

Related reading: learn how to spot polybutylene pipes in Florida and when pinhole leaks in copper pipes point to a repipe. Older steel lines are covered in the galvanized pipe replacement guide.

When should you call a repiping professional?

Call a pro when:

  • You've had two or more leaks in a year
  • Your home has polybutylene or galvanized supply pipe
  • You see rusty water, low flow or green stains at fittings
  • An insurer or buyer asks about your pipes

Frequently asked questions

How long does a whole house repipe take?

Many homes take a few days, depending on size and access. Ask whether water will be on each night.

Does a repipe add value to a home?

It can make a home easier to insure and sell, especially if it replaces polybutylene. Keep the permit and invoice for buyers.

Is PEX cheaper than copper for a repipe?

Usually, yes. PEX costs less and installs faster because it bends around corners with fewer fittings.

Can I repipe one part of the house?

Yes. A partial repipe can replace one section, such as a bathroom group or the lines under a slab. It may cost less now but leave older pipe in place.

Do I need to move out during a repipe?

Most people stay home. Expect noise, dust and water shut-offs during work hours.
